Cervical radiculopathy/myelopathy is strongly disfavored by symmetry, lack of sensory findings, reflex changes, or neck symptoms — and EMG/NCS will readily exclude focal neurogenic causes.

[EVIDENCE]  
- Gradual-onset, symmetric proximal upper extremity weakness over several months  
- Functional impairment limited to shoulder girdle (difficulty combing hair, reaching overhead)  
- Absence of constitutional symptoms (fever, weight loss, night sweats)  
- Absence of skin/mucosal findings, arthralgias/arthritis, dysphagia, dysarthria  
- No lower extremity weakness  
- No myalgia, tenderness, swelling, or rash in shoulders/upper arms  
- Normal CBC (nonspecific but argues against acute systemic inflammation or hematologic malignancy)  
- EMG/NCS ordered — appropriate next step to confirm myopathic pattern  
- Muscle biopsy (deltoid) planned — consistent with suspicion for primary myopathy  

[GAPS]  
- Serum creatine kinase (CK) result — critical to assess for myofiber injury; normal CK would reduce likelihood of active inflammatory myopathy but not exclude IMNM or chronic cases  
- EMG/NCS results — needed to confirm myopathic vs. neurogenic pattern and rule out multifocal neuropathy or radicular involvement  
- Manual muscle testing (MRC scale) — required to quantify severity and distribution (e.g., deltoid, supraspinatus, biceps, triceps strength)  
- 25-hydroxyvitamin D level — vitamin D deficiency can cause proximal myopathy, though usually subacute and reversible, and often with nonspecific myalgia (absent here)  
- ESR/CRP — nonspecific but supportive of inflammation if elevated  
- Muscle MRI (if CK elevated or EMG equivocal) — to assess for edema/fatty replacement pattern (e.g., selective involvement of deltoid, infraspinatus, serratus anterior in IIM)  

[DIAGNOSIS]  
Inflammatory myopathy (most consistent with immune-mediated necrotizing myopathy or polymyositis)
